title: How to build a grading rubric in Google Forms on Mac, step by step for teachers
metaTitle: Build a Grading Rubric in Google Forms on Mac
description: Build a grading rubric in Google Forms on Mac without buying anything. Criteria, four levels, a worked example and a routine for grading faster.
targetKeyword: build a grading rubric in google forms
intro: To build a grading rubric in Google Forms, list your criteria, write four levels for each one, then turn each criterion into a question with the levels as choices. Forms collects the answers in a linked Google Sheet. Here is how to do that on a Mac, and where the time actually goes.
tldr: Write the criteria before the levels. Most rubrics fail because two criteria describe the same flaw.
Describe each level with things a reader can see, not with words like good or clear.
Build the rubric as a table in Google Docs first, then copy the finished wording into a Form for scoring.
Share the rubric before students start. Keep one master copy and reuse it next term.

blocks.text: A grading rubric is a grid. Each row is one thing you grade, and each column is one level of quality. The grid looks small. It is not small when you build one for every class and every assignment. A typical teacher works about 54 hours a week, and direct teaching is just under half of that, according to a 2022 EdWeek Research Center survey of more than 1,300 teachers.
What a rubric costs you right now

Rubric work rarely shows up on a timesheet. It shows up on a Sunday evening. In a Massachusetts study of 19 teachers, the typical weekend total for grading, lesson planning and other school work was 3.85 hours. Those were self-estimates, and the authors say they may be biased upward. The pattern is worth taking seriously anyway.

Burnout adds weight to every hour. RAND's 2025 State of the American Teacher survey found that 53% of teachers reported burnout, down from 60%. A rubric will not fix that. But each hour spent rebuilding the same criteria for the same assignment is an hour you did not need to spend.

rows: A blank page at the start of every term, for every assignment
Two papers that look alike get different marks on different days
Comments such as needs more detail, with no level and no example
Students ask what a B required, and the answer lives only in your head
blocks.caption: Four costs you pay when a rubric is missing or vague.

blocks.text: Why rubrics take so long to build

Most of the time goes to wording, not the grid. You can draw a table in a few minutes. Writing four honest levels for each criterion takes longer. The usual trap is criteria that overlap. Organization and structure often mean the same thing, so you penalize one flaw twice. Then the scores stop matching what you meant.
Step by step: build the grading rubric before Google Forms

Build the rubric in a document first. Google Forms is for collecting answers. Fixing wording in a table is faster than editing a form with a dozen questions. Use Google Docs for the draft, then copy the finished wording into the Form.

items: Pull three pieces of graded work. Choose one strong, one middle and one weak sample.
Write what you noticed in plain phrases, such as claim in the first paragraph or cites a source for each point.
Group the phrases into three to five criteria. Merge any two that point at the same flaw.
Name each criterion with a short noun, such as Evidence, Claim or Conventions.
Write the middle level first, then the top and bottom. Four levels is enough to separate strong work from weak work.
Check every level for words a reader can see. A student should be able to point at the sentence that proves the level.
Set weights if the grade is points. In Microsoft Teams, weights should total 100%.
Test the rubric on your three samples. Rewrite any level where two samples land there for different reasons.

blocks.text: In Google Docs, use Insert > Table. Put the criteria in the first column and one column for each level. Type the descriptors into the cells, and keep each cell short enough to read at a glance. Here is a worked example for one criterion in a short argument essay.

rows: Uses several sources, explains how each supports the claim, and names one limit of the evidence.
Uses at least two sources, and links each one to the claim in a sentence.
Uses sources, but one is dropped in with no link to the claim.
Gives an opinion with no source, or cites a source that does not support the claim.
blocks.caption: One criterion, Evidence, written at four levels.

blocks.text: Notice what is missing. No level says good or weak. Each one names something a reader can check. That difference decides whether the rubric speeds up grading or starts arguments. Words like strong and clear describe a feeling, so two graders will read them differently.
Move the rubric into a Google Form for scoring

Once the grid is set, open Google Forms and start a new form. Make one question per criterion. Use a multiple choice or dropdown question for the level, and list the four level names as the choices. Add a short answer question under each one for a comment. The grader fills in one form per student, and the answers land in a linked Google Sheet.

Put the level descriptors in the description under each question, so the grader can read them while scoring. Long descriptors inside the answer choices make the form hard to read. Keep the choices short, such as Beyond or Meets, and let the description hold the detail.

blocks.title: Forms records, Sheets adds up
blocks.text: Forms records the answers. It will not total a rubric for you. If you want a score, add a formula in the linked Sheet, then check it by hand against two or three papers before you trust it.
Google Classroom, Teams and Gradescope rubric options

If your class already runs in Google Classroom, you may not need a Form at all. Classroom has its own rubric tool. It allows up to 50 criteria and up to 10 levels per criterion. You can reuse a rubric across assignments, and edits do not change the original. Once grading starts, the rubric cannot be edited or deleted, so finish the wording first. Android and tablets can only view rubrics, so edit on a computer.

Microsoft Teams Assignments can create a rubric manually or with AI. Microsoft says the first AI output often needs revision. Teams can download rubrics as CSV or Word files and upload CSV files. Gradescope Basic is free after the Institutional trial and includes Dynamic Rubrics. Importing and lockable rubrics are Institutional features, so check what your school pays for before you plan around them.
Mistakes people make with grading rubrics

items: Writing levels as quality words. Excellent and good tell a student nothing they can act on.
Grading the same flaw in two criteria, so one weak paragraph costs points twice.
Building the rubric after grading starts. Early papers then get a different standard than the last ones.
Showing the rubric only after the work is due, so students cannot aim at it.
Letting students grade themselves for marks. Self-grading tends to inflate scores, so keep it separate from grades.
Keeping the only copy inside a Form. Save the wording in a Doc as well.

blocks.text: What the research says about rubric scoring

The evidence is useful, but it is modest. Jonsson and Svingby reviewed 75 empirical studies. They found rubrics make scoring more consistent, especially when the rubric is analytic, topic specific and paired with exemplars or rater training. They also concluded that a rubric does not make a judgment valid by itself.

A 2023 meta-analysis by Panadero and colleagues reported a moderate effect on academic performance, g = 0.45, across 21 studies. The effects on self-regulated learning and self-efficacy were small, and their confidence intervals include zero. A rubric is a tool for clarity. It is not a guarantee of better learning.

blocks.title: Check the self-efficacy numbers
blocks.text: One abstract page prints a self-efficacy interval that looks asymmetric around its estimate. Read the full text before you cite that figure.

Andrade's work on self-assessment fits your daily routine more closely. Students can grade their own draft against the rubric, as long as the self-grade is not counted and students get time to revise. In one older study, students who self-assessed with a rubric averaged a low B. The comparison group averaged a high C. Those studies are small, so treat them as a reason to try, not as proof.
Keep a master copy and reuse it next term

Save the finished rubric as one master Doc. Name it with the subject, the assignment type and the year. For each new assignment, make a copy and edit the copy. Leave the master alone. Change one criterion at a time when you revise, so you can compare scores across terms.
Share the rubric before students start the work

Give students the rubric when you assign the work, not after they submit. Walk through one sample with the class. Andrade's steps include analyzing a sample, grouping qualities into criteria and drafting four levels. Self-assessment can take one or two class periods. Then give time to revise, because students need to act on what they find.
Student data and what Lazur can see

Building a rubric is safe. A Form full of student names is a different thing. Follow your school's rules on student records before you paste names, grades or work into any tool. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. When Lazur answers, the audio and screenshot go to AI providers. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models.
If a screen shows student records, close that window or move it off screen before you hold the shortcut. That is the simplest rule, and it costs nothing.
Next steps for your rubric this week

Pick the assignment you grade most often. Build one rubric for it, following the steps above. Test it on three papers you already graded. Mark every place where your old score and the new level disagree. Those are the descriptors to fix first. For the rest of your Google Docs setup, see [Google Docs for teachers on Mac](/for/teachers/google-docs).

faq.question: Does Google Forms have a rubric builder?
faq.answer: This page treats Forms as a scoring form, not a rubric builder. Build the grid in a Google Doc first. Then turn each criterion into a Form question, with the levels as choices.

faq.question: How many criteria should one rubric have?
faq.answer: Keep it short enough to score in one pass. Google Classroom allows up to 50 criteria and up to 10 levels per criterion. Those are ceilings, not targets. More criteria usually mean more overlap and more time per paper.

faq.question: Should I use four levels or five?
faq.answer: Andrade's steps call for drafting four levels. Four is enough to separate strong work from weak work without splitting hairs between neighboring levels. Use five only if your descriptors stay observable at every level.

faq.question: Do rubrics really save grading time?
faq.answer: Cornell's teaching guide says rubrics save grading time in the short and long term. That is practical guidance, not a measured result. Expect the first rubric to take longer. The savings show up when you reuse it.

faq.question: Should students see the rubric before they start?
faq.answer: Yes. Share it when you assign the work. Keep student self-grades separate from the official grade, since students tend to inflate their own scores.

faq.question: Can I put student names into Lazur?
faq.answer: Follow your school's rules on student records first. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer and are not stored.

faq.question: Can I reuse a rubric next term?
faq.answer: Yes. In Google Classroom, edits to a reused rubric do not change the original. Keep a master copy in Google Docs anyway, so the wording survives any change of tool.

costs.title: Hours after school
costs.text: Rubric work adds to a week that is already long. The 54 hour figure covers all teacher work, and rubric building is one slice of it. The real cost is repetition. A rubric you rebuild each term charges you every term.

costs.title: Scores that drift
costs.text: Vague criteria push a grader to decide by feel. Two sessions of grading can then disagree with each other. Jonsson and Svingby found rubrics make scoring more consistent, especially when they are specific.

costs.title: Feedback students skip
costs.text: A comment that says needs more detail gives no path forward. Students read the grade and move on. Level descriptors name the next step, so the feedback does real work.

costs.title: Arguments about grades
costs.text: When the standard lives only in your head, every grade becomes a debate. Students ask what the B required. A written rubric answers that question before it comes up.

causes.title: Criteria that overlap
causes.text: Two criteria that describe the same flaw make the rubric count it twice. Organization and structure are a common pair. Each one gets a score, so one weak paragraph costs points twice. Check each criterion against the others and remove the overlap.

causes.title: Levels described by feeling
causes.text: Words like strong, clear and good describe a grader's impression, not evidence. Each level needs something a reader can see. Without that, the descriptors cannot separate one level from the next.

causes.title: No model paper
causes.text: Many teachers write levels before they read any student work. The levels then describe an ideal, not the work in front of them. Test the wording on real samples to close that gap.

causes.title: Starting from a blank page each term
causes.text: Without a master copy, each rubric starts from zero. Teachers repeat the same wording work every term. The fix is one reusable copy that changes slowly.

causes.title: Writing the rubric while grading
causes.text: A rubric written during grading tends to match the papers already read. Early papers and late papers then get different standards. Finish the wording before the first paper is scored.

fixes.title: Write four levels with visible features
fixes.text: Use phrases a reader can check, such as cites two sources in the body or states a claim in the first paragraph. Avoid strong, weak and clear on their own. Andrade's steps call for drafting four levels, which is enough to separate strong work from weak work.

fixes.title: Test on three samples first
fixes.text: Pick one strong, one middle and one weak paper. Score each one with the new rubric. If two samples land in one level for different reasons, rewrite that descriptor until the difference shows on the page.

fixes.title: Keep one master Doc
fixes.text: Store the wording in a Google Doc table, so you can copy it for each assignment. Google Classroom can also export a rubric to Google Sheets, which lets you share it with colleagues outside the class.

fixes.title: Use the Form only for the scoring pass
fixes.text: Build and revise in Docs. Once the wording is locked, copy it into a Google Form. The Form records the grader's choices, and the linked Sheet keeps every answer in one place.

fixes.title: Share the rubric before the work starts
fixes.text: Give the rubric when you assign the work. Students who know the target can aim at it. Andrade suggests one or two class periods for self-assessment, followed by time to revise.

fixes.title: Pair the level with one next step
fixes.text: Pick the level in the Form, then add one line on the next step. A line that says move your evidence into the body gives the student a task. Hold fn to dictate that line, so you can speak it instead of typing it.

lazurHelps.say: Ask Lazur to explain what separates Meets from Approaching in your rubric.
lazurHelps.result: Lazur explains the difference out loud, based on what is on your screen, so you can rewrite the descriptor.

lazurHelps.say: Ask Lazur to draft four level descriptors for one criterion.
lazurHelps.result: You get a draft to edit and check against your own standard. Lazur does not put the text into your Form.

lazurHelps.say: Ask Lazur where the add question button is in this Form.
lazurHelps.result: Lazur circles the control and labels it. You do the clicking.

lazurHelps.say: Ask Lazur to walk you through a dropdown question, one click at a time.
lazurHelps.result: Lazur guides one click at a time and waits for each click before it goes on.

lazurHelps.say: Hold fn and dictate the feedback line for one student.
lazurHelps.result: Dictation writes clean text at the cursor in any app, so feedback goes into the Form or Doc without typing.

plan.label: Monday
plan.title: Pull sample work
plan.text: Pick three graded pieces: one strong, one middle, one weak. Write down what separates the strong one from the weak one in plain phrases.

plan.label: Tuesday
plan.title: Group into criteria
plan.text: Merge overlapping phrases into three to five criteria. Give each criterion a short noun name, such as Evidence or Conventions. Remove any criterion that repeats another.

plan.label: Wednesday
plan.title: Write the levels
plan.text: In a Google Doc table, write the middle level first, then the top and bottom. Check each cell for words a reader can see. Read the rubric aloud once.

plan.label: Thursday
plan.title: Pilot and fix
plan.text: Score one student paper with the rubric. If the score feels wrong, find the descriptor that caused it and rewrite that cell only.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Build the Form
plan.text: Copy the locked wording into a Google Form, one question per criterion. Save the Doc as the master copy and note what to change next term.
